The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven for hours to reach the coast, and when we finally stepped onto the sand, the world felt different—bigger, louder, alive in a way I couldn’t explain. The waves crashed against the shore like they were trying to tell me something, and I stood there, barefoot, letting the water lap at my toes. It wasn’t just the vastness of the water that struck me; it was the way it moved, relentless and free, as if it had no choice but to keep going.

Years later, I still find myself drawn to the ocean. There’s a kind of peace in its chaos, a reminder that not everything can be controlled. The tides rise and fall without apology, the currents shift without warning, and yet, it’s all part of a rhythm older than time. Sometimes, when the world feels too loud or too heavy, I close my eyes and imagine standing at the edge again, letting the salt spray kiss my face.

The ocean teaches patience. It doesn’t rush. It doesn’t beg for attention. It simply *is*—powerful, mysterious, and indifferent to the small dramas of human life. And maybe that’s why I love it. In a world that demands we be busy, productive, *useful*, the ocean is a quiet rebellion. It doesn’t care if you’re important or if your plans are perfect. It just rolls in, over and over, as it always has.

I wonder if, deep down, we’re all a little like the ocean—trying to find our way, crashing against the shore of life, only to be pulled back again. Maybe that’s the real magic of it.
